text: What is an operating system, and why do we need one?
expectedAnswerPoints: System software acting as an intermediary between user applications and hardware
Without it every application would need its own hardware-handling code, making programs large and duplicated
Provides controlled resource allocation so one program cannot monopolise CPU, memory or I/O
Provides memory protection so processes cannot corrupt each other's memory
Core functions include process management, memory management, file system management, device management and security

text: What is a kernel? Explain the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel.
expectedAnswerPoints: The kernel is the part of the OS that interacts directly with hardware and performs the most critical tasks
Monolithic: the entire OS runs as one large program in kernel mode (e.g. Linux, UNIX)
Microkernel: only essential services run in kernel mode, the rest run in user mode (e.g. MINIX, Mach)
Monolithic is faster because there are fewer mode switches between components
Microkernel is more stable and secure because a failing service does not bring down the kernel

text: What is a system call, and why can a user program not access hardware directly?
expectedAnswerPoints: A mechanism by which a user program requests a service from the kernel that it lacks permission to perform itself
User programs run in restricted user mode and cannot directly access I/O devices or other processes' memory
A system call triggers a controlled switch from user mode to kernel mode
Categories include process control, file management, device management, information maintenance and communication
Examples: fork, exec, open, read, write, exit

text: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode, and why does the distinction exist?
expectedAnswerPoints: Kernel mode is privileged, with full access to hardware and all system resources
User mode is restricted, with limited access to system resources
Applications normally run in user mode
The separation prevents a buggy or malicious program from crashing or compromising the whole system
Switching to kernel mode happens via system calls, interrupts or exceptions

text: What is a Process Control Block (PCB), and why does the OS need one per process?
expectedAnswerPoints: A data structure holding all information about a process: process ID, state, program counter, CPU registers, memory limits, open files
Each process has its own PCB; the collection of PCBs forms the process table
Enables context switching by storing the exact state needed to pause and resume a process
Lets the OS track and manage many processes at once, which multiprogramming requires
Stored in protected kernel memory, inaccessible to user-mode programs

text: What is context switching, and why is it considered overhead?
expectedAnswerPoints: Saving the state of the currently running process and restoring the state of another process that is ready to run
The CPU saves registers and program counter into the current process's PCB, then loads the next process's context from its PCB
It is overhead because no useful user work is done during the switch
Enables multitasking, fair CPU sharing and responsiveness to interactive tasks
Cost depends on the number of registers to save/restore, memory speed and hardware support

text: Describe the states a process can be in during its lifetime.
expectedAnswerPoints: New: the process is being created and resources are being set up
Ready: waiting to be assigned to the CPU
Running: currently executing on the CPU
Waiting/Blocked: waiting for an I/O operation or event to complete
Terminated: execution finished or the process was killed, and resources are released
Suspended: temporarily swapped out, can return to ready or waiting later

text: What is the difference between user-level threads and kernel-level threads?
expectedAnswerPoints: User-level threads are managed by a user-space thread library; the kernel is unaware of them
Kernel-level threads are created and scheduled by the operating system
User-level context switching is faster because it needs no kernel involvement
If one user-level thread blocks on a system call, the whole process can block; with kernel threads only that thread blocks
Kernel threads can be scheduled across multiple CPU cores for true parallelism

text: Compare FCFS, Shortest Job First and Round Robin CPU scheduling, including their drawbacks.
expectedAnswerPoints: FCFS runs processes in arrival order; simple but suffers the convoy effect where short jobs wait behind long ones
SJF picks the smallest burst time first and is optimal for average waiting time
SJF requires knowing burst times in advance and can starve long processes
Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum in cyclic order, which suits time-sharing systems
Round Robin with too small a quantum causes excessive context-switching overhead; too large and it degenerates towards FCFS

text: What is a race condition, and what is a critical section?
expectedAnswerPoints: A race condition occurs when multiple processes access and modify shared data concurrently and the result depends on execution order
The outcome is unpredictable and may differ between runs
A critical section is the part of the code where shared resources are accessed
Only one process should execute its critical section at a time
A correct solution must provide mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting

text: What is a semaphore? Explain the difference between binary and counting semaphores.
expectedAnswerPoints: A synchronisation primitive (an integer counter) used to control access to shared resources
Two atomic operations: wait/P decrements and blocks if the value would go negative, signal/V increments and may wake a blocked process
A binary semaphore takes only 0 or 1 and behaves like a lock
A counting semaphore takes any non-negative value and is used when several identical resources exist
The operations must be atomic, otherwise the semaphore itself becomes a race condition

text: What is virtual memory, and how does demand paging work?
expectedAnswerPoints: Virtual memory lets a system run programs larger than physical RAM by using disk space as an extension of memory
Each process gets its own virtual address space, which also provides isolation between processes
In demand paging, pages are loaded into memory only when they are actually referenced
Referencing a page that is not in memory causes a page fault, and the OS loads it from disk
Saves memory and speeds up program startup, but frequent page faults are expensive

text: Explain the difference between internal and external fragmentation, and how each is addressed.
expectedAnswerPoints: Internal fragmentation is wasted space inside an allocated block, when a process is given more memory than it uses
External fragmentation is wasted space between allocated blocks: enough total memory is free but it is scattered in pieces too small to use
Internal fragmentation arises with fixed partitioning and is reduced by variable partitioning or paging
External fragmentation arises with variable partitioning and is addressed by compaction or paging
Paging largely eliminates external fragmentation because any free frame can hold any page

text: Compare FIFO, LRU and Optimal page replacement algorithms, and explain Belady's anomaly.
expectedAnswerPoints: FIFO evicts the oldest loaded page; simple to implement with a queue but may evict a frequently used page
LRU evicts the page unused for the longest time; a good approximation of real behaviour but needs usage tracking
Optimal evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in future; best possible but requires future knowledge
Optimal is not implementable and is used only as a benchmark
Belady's anomaly is when increasing the number of frames increases the number of page faults
Belady's anomaly can occur with FIFO but not with LRU or Optimal, which are stack algorithms

text: What is thrashing? What causes it and how can it be resolved?
expectedAnswerPoints: Thrashing is when the system spends more time swapping pages in and out than executing useful work
Caused by too many processes competing for too little physical memory
Each process lacks its working set, so page faults become constant
Symptom is high CPU utilisation with very low actual throughput
Fixes include reducing the degree of multiprogramming, using the working set model, and adding more physical memory
